articles.headline: Fantasy Baseball Offseason Tracker: Kevin Gausman gets prove-it deal from Tigers; Alec Bohm goes to Royals
keyFacts: Before a potential baseball lockout halts transactions, several major MLB players have agreed to new contracts with various teams for the upcoming season.
Notable signings include Tarik Skubal joining the Mets for nine years and $450 million, and Trevor Rogers signing a five-year, $120 million deal with the Cubs.
Writers Scott White and Chris Towers analyzed these offseason moves and provided fantasy baseball impact breakdowns for each newly signed player.
body: A lockout may be coming, but nobody told the hot stove. It's already burning bright with even the biggest prize, two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, coming off the market. Trevor Rogers and Freddy Peralta soon followed, and at this rate, most of the marquee free agents will be nailed down by Thanksgiving.

There's a reason for the urgency. Once the lockout becomes official, the signings -- and all other transactions -- will cease, but those that occur before then will still count toward the date when baseball is allowed to resume. So we'd better document them all here, just like any other offseason, breaking down their impact for Fantasy Baseball.

That's what Scott White and Chris Towers intend to do over the next few weeks, at least, before everything goes quiet. They'll eventually pick up where they left off when the hot stove heats up again in ... March? Hopefully not much later than that.
Whatever the timeline, you'll want this page bookmarked so you can get the first word on everything that happens.
Kevin Gausman signs with Tigers

You would think a pitcher entering the twilight of his career at age 36 would hold out for a multi-year deal, but Gausman ultimately had to settle for a one-year, $25 million contract with the Tigers. That's because his 4.51 ERA was his highest since 2019, which was before he became a front-line option with the Giants and Blue Jays.

Things went from bad to worse for him after he was dealt to the Cubs at the trade deadline last season. Granted, there were some confounding data points, such as his 3.74 FIP and improvement in both strikeout rate and average exit velocity, but the simple fact is that his overall production has been trending down for a few years now. If one change of scenery -- which provided as good of a defense as a pitcher could ask for, by the way -- wasn't enough to set him straight, then the odds are against this one being much better. There remains some sneaky upside for Gausman, but the probability of him meeting it is too low for him to place inside of my top 60 starting pitchers. --Scott White
Foster Griffin signs with Guardians

What's so interesting about this signing is that the Guardians got the short end of the stick in Griffin's otherwise successful return from Japan. The left-hander put together a 5.19 ERA and 1.62 WHIP in his nine starts for them compared to 3.06 and 1.08 in his 22 starts for the Nationals. Of course, he actually had a lower FIP in his Guardians starts (3.54) than his Nationals starts (4.10), which underscores the role that chance played in the distribution.

Ultimately, the Guardians liked what they saw and decided to re-up with Griffin for three more years. Should we do the same in Fantasy? Look, he's not winning 15 games again, and that ended up being the basis of his value after his percentages took a turn for the worse. The control wasn't as steady as it needed to be for him to be a real asset, but he surrenders weak contact and registers strikeouts at an OK clip. The upside isn't especially high, but he's the sort of late-round target who could deliver a mid-round outcome if everything breaks right. --Scott White
Alec Bohm signs with Royals

I've got to hand it to Bohm. I didn't think he'd be able to find a full-time role on the open market as a right-handed-hitting corner man with modest power, limited on-base skills and poor defense. To my surprise, though, he ends up latching on with a Royals team that suddenly found itself in need of a third baseman after dealing away Maikel Garcia for Bryce Miller. So I guess this means we need to continue caring about Bohm in Fantasy, at least to the degree that this park downgrade allows for.

Unfortunately, it may be the nail in the coffin for him as a power hitter. Nearly 60 percent of Bohm's 85 career home runs have come at homer-friendly Citizens Bank Park, and Kauffman Stadium is on the other end of the spectrum as far as that goes. A change in configuration last year may have closed the gap some, but there was already so little margin for error in Bohm's case. A scenario exists in which he sells out more for batting average in a stadium with more outfield ground to cover -- that's typically been his best trait anyway -- but I don't know that you can expect even double-digit home runs from him over the next couple years. He'll have some late-round appeal as a category stabilizer in Rotisserie leagues. He might have even more value in points leagues, thanks to his low strikeout rate, but those tend not to go as deep into the player pool. --Scott White
Tyler Stephenson signs with Reds

Stephenson tested the free agent market and apparently found it not to his liking. He's back with the organization where he just spent the past six-plus seasons, agreeing Tuesday to a three-year, $30 million deal with the Reds. He does have an opt out after the first two seasons, and by that point, stud prospect Alfredo Duno may be ready to take over by the plate. This deal permits the soon-to-be 21-year-old the leeway to develop fully. As for Stephenson, we know what to expect from him with the Reds. They play in as favorable of a home run venue as there is, which I suppose makes this signing good news, though Stephenson's home/away splits have run pretty even throughout his career unenticing overall. He's a serviceable enough second catcher for Rotisserie leagues, capable of hitting 15 home runs with a batting average that won't kill you, but unless you get squeezed out at the position, you'd prefer to target someone higher-upside on Draft Day. --Scott White
Kaima Taira signs with Blue Jays

If Taira makes 20 starts in 2027, he'll be just the second pitcher in the past 40 years to do so while listed at 5-foot-8 or below – Marcus Stroman, of course, did it eight times between 2014 and 2024. That alone tells you how unique Taira is. Taira spent much of his career in Japan jumping between the bullpen and the rotation, and he found success as both a closer and, more recently, a frontline starter, coming off a season where he threw 146 innings of 23 starts with a 1.36 ERA. Despite his diminutive size and merely-good 25% strikeout rate, Taira sits in the mid-90s with his fastball, and it plays up even more because he somehow manages to generate 6.8 feet of extension when he releases the ball.

As we have come to expect from pitchers coming over from Japan, Taira features a full arsenal, with a slider, cutter, curveball, changeup, and splitter, and he improved his command across the board in 2026 en route to a career-best 7.9% walk rate. After signing for five years and $80 million (with an opt-out after the third season), Taira seems all but certain to open the 2027 season in the Blue Jays rotation. Whether he stays there for good will depend on how he acclimates to the majors, and as Tatsuya Imai showed us last season, that's no guarantee. But Taima has the talent and contract of a major-league starter, and potentially a pretty good one. He's a viable reserve rounds target for 2027 drafts. --Chris Towers
Freddy Peralta signs with Orioles

The Orioles basically swapped out Trevor Rogers for Peralta while getting an extra first-round pick out of the deal, and given that the talent disparity between the two seems pretty minimal, it's a reasonable move. But if the Orioles aren't getting a downgrade in talent, they might be taking on some more volatility and putting a bit more pressure on the bullpen. Rogers has averaged 5.8 innings per start over the past two seasons while Peralta is at 5.3.

Peralta struggled through a very tough 2026, especially with the Mets, who tried to change his delivery and were rewarded with a 4.99 ERA in 22 starts. Things were better for him with the Rays, though that was at least in part due to the better defense around him. They did, however, manage to unlock a bunch of extra velocity in the playoffs especially, where he put up a 2.95 ERA in 21.1 innings. The strikeouts still weren't there and the control took a step back, but if Peralta can sustain a fastball more in the 96 mph range than 94, you can expect the strikeouts to be fine. The right-hander has long been a volatile pitcher, but 2026 was the first time his ERA ended up on the wrong side of 4.00 since 2019. He was overdrafted as an ace in 2026, but as a mid-range SP with 200-strikeout upside, he's a decent pick at his current 137.8 ADP. --Chris Towers
Kris Bubic signs with Guardians

Bubic is really good. Over his past 217.1 innings of work, he has a 2.98 ERA, 227 strikeouts, and 1.17 WHIP. That's a viable option in any team's rotation … for as long as he can remain in the rotation. Unfortunately, it's never for very long before injuries inevitably catch up to him; those 217.1 innings cover the 2023 through 2026 seasons. In 2025, he made 20 starts before his season ended in July with a rotator cuff strain, and then he managed nine starts before a left elbow issue ended his run as a starter in 2026 (he re-emerged in September as a single-inning reliever for the Dodgers).

If the market thought Bubic could hold up as a full-time starter, he definitely wouldn't be settling for a one-year deal, but since he signed with the Guardians, who wouldn't be willing to shell out the money required for a safer choice, we can feel confident he'll get another chance in the role. He's a very solid bench piece for Fantasy drafts and should be worth having in your lineup as long as he's healthy enough to pitch. Just don't expect that to be for very long. --Chris Towers
Teruaki Sato signs with Cubs

Sato joins the Cubs after a standout career with the Hanshin Tigers in Japan. He won the 2025 Central League MVP and is widely expected to win his second in a row after securing the Triple Crown in 2026. The Cubs are, for all intents and purposes, swapping out Seiya Suzuki for Sato, but can Sato be as good as Suzuki? The upside is there, but the Cubs are taking on quite a bit of risk in this swap. Sato clearly has power, hitting a combined 79 home runs over the past two seasons, but he also struck out 27% of the time during that time. In contrast, Suzuki never struck out more than 22% of the time while in Japan and yet has run a 25% strikeout rate throughout his major league career. For more, . --Chris Towers
Trevor Rogers signs with Cubs

Maybe you thought Sonny Gray's two-year, $55 million deal with the Twins was too little. Maybe you thought Tarik Skubal's nine-year, $450 million deal with the Mets was too much. Does that make Rogers' five-year, $120 million deal with the Cubs just right? For me, maybe, since I rank him 36th at starting pitcher, but early ADP has him going only 53rd, behind the likes of Nick Pivetta and Christian Scott. It's clear, then, that Fantasy Baseballers, at least the kind that participate in November NFBC drafts, don't regard Rogers as highly as the game at large does. A big reason for that, I think, is that he had an ERA over 4.00 in 2026, which most Roto rating systems regard as an albatross around a pitcher's neck, but perhaps a better indicator of the way he pitched was his 3.45 FIP.

Even that doesn't entirely do him justice. He has a 3.16 ERA, 1.07 WHIP and 8.4 K/9 in 48 starts over the past two seasons and had a 2.90 ERA, 1.03 WHIP and 8.9 K/9 over his final 20 starts in 2026. Sure, he was bad early on -- so much that his breakthrough 2025 was written off as a fluke in some corners -- but I suspect that a bout with the flu -- one so severe that it landed him on the IL for two weeks in April and May -- also had a deleterious effect on his mechanics. Once he got them sorted out, he was a top-of-the-rotation arm again, and that's how he spent the majority of his 2026. It doesn't hurt either that the Cubs ranked a distant No. 1 in defensive runs saved last year. The Orioles, by comparison, were middle of the pack. Let this be your reminder not to underrate Rogers in drafts, as so many are. --Scott White
Tarik Skubal signs with Mets

At nine years, $450 million, Skubal's contract with the Mets is the biggest ever for a pitcher, bettering the $325 million deal that the Dodgers gave Yoshinobu Yamamoto prior to the 2024 season. So does it confirm he's the SP1 for 2027, ahead of even Jacob Misiorowski? There's at least a case for it, even with the Mets' reputation for being the Wile E. Coyote of baseball teams, by which I mean doomed to see every state-of-the-art purchase blow up in their face. For more, check out my full-length article. --Scott White
Royce Lewis traded to Dodgers

At first glance, this looks like the nail in the coffin for a player whose Fantasy value has already been in free fall, but Lewis can play all over the diamond and the Dodgers have no shortage of geriatric players. He may not play as consistently as he did with the Twins, but between spelling Max Muncy at third base, spelling Freddie Freeman at first base, and filling in for whatever injury pops up, Lewis should play enough to be of some use in Rotisserie leagues, with their larger lineups.

And that's all you should have been counting on anyway with the way his numbers have trended since 2024. He made such a splash to begin his career that it seemed like only injuries would hold him back, but he's shown himself to be just a .230 hitter over the past three years. Maybe with consistent playing time, he could eke out 20 homers, particularly now that he's in a more favorable venue for him, but again, his playing time is about to be less consistent, not more. --Scott White
Maikel Garcia traded to Mariners

This is a trade that makes a ton of sense for real-life baseball but might be a disaster for Fantasy. The Mariners got -0.5 WAR from their third basemen in 2026, per FanGraphs, and Garcia represents a significant upgrade from that. As recently as 2025, put up a .286/.351/.449 line and was a borderline elite Fantasy option as a result.

Unfortunately for our purposes, this trade makes it a lot less likely he'll live up to that level of play in 2027. Kauffman Stadium in Kansas City suppresses homers but is generally a pretty good offensive environment, sporting the seventh-best park factor for hitters, per BaseballSavant.com. T-Mobile Park in Seattle? It's the worst hitter's park in baseball by a pretty wide margin, though how that impacts each individual hitter often varies. Randy Arozarena more or less held serve in his time in Seattle, while someone like Eugenio Suarez struggled mightily in both stints there. It's something about the way hitters see the ball and how the humid, often chilly atmosphere affects batted balls' trajectories. There just isn't another offensive environment in baseball quite like T-Mobile Park, and it generally serves as a drag on offense across the board.

If Garcia can hit like he did in 2025, he'll still be very fantasy-relevant, however. That season saw Garcia max out his power, bumping his average exit velocity to 91.3 mph, while also increasing his launch angle, allowing him to tap into far more of that power than ever before. That he did it without sacrificing his superlative contact skills made for a very strong package. But he gave back nearly all of those improvements in 2026 and returned to being a roughly average hitter. He struggled while playing through injuries to his left hand and wrist before eventually going on the IL for nearly two months, then struggled with hamstring issues late in the season. If the injuries explain his struggles, then betting on a bounceback makes sense, even in Seattle.

But 2025 might have just been a career year, and the move to T-Mobile Park makes it even less likely he'll get back to that level. Garcia's price has already slipped to 169.4 in early NFBC drafts, but I'd expect it to drop even farther after this. He's a fringe starting-caliber third baseman for Fantasy, and I'd take at least Curtis Mead and Isaac Paredes ahead of him, among players with a current lower ADP. --Chris Towers
Bryce Miller traded to the Royals

While Maikel Garcia is going to the worst hitter's park in the league, Miller suffers from the opposite move, exiting one of the best pitching environments in the league. It's one he has specifically benefited from, sporting a career 3.49 ERA at home compared to a 4.63 ERA on the road. It would be overly simplistic to say he has lost whatever Fantasy relevance he had with this move, but it might not end up wrong.

To add some nuance, I think Miller can be a good pitcher in any offensive environment; he just hasn't been for long. He's had stretches across different seasons where he has looked like an ace, but he never manages to sustain it. He has pitched through various elbow issues over the years, but when he is right, he rides a high-vert, high-velo fastball to very good results. Let's not forget that he started the 2026 season with a 1.71 ERA and 10.6 K/9 in his first eight starts, but then he tried pitching through a lat issue and wasn't the same. Still, it was another reminder of how good he can be at his best. Given the inconsistency and the park downgrade, Miller should continue to see his price fall. He's down to 266.3 in those early NFBC drafts and should probably just be a reserve round dart throw now that he's with the Royals. --Chris Towers
Sonny Gray signs with the Twins

It's not the first place I would have bet on Gray signing, but the Twins have made it clear since the most recent trade deadline that they aren't looking to rebuild. The deal is officially for one year but includes a 2028 player option for the 37-year-old Gray, meaning the Twins will either be happy about getting one great season out of him or will be looking at a fairly onerous (but short!) deal for 2028. It's a tradeoff worth making for a team like the Twins, who have talent in the rotation but little in the way of sure things, either from a performance or a health perspective. Gray is seemingly a different type of pitcher every season, but from a real-life perspective, it's easy to see the appeal in employing him: He has made at least 24 starts in every season since 2017 (minus the shortened 2020 season) and has had an ERA over 4.00 just twice in his past eight seasons.

From a Fantasy perspective, his value is a little less clear. He had an excellent 2026 season that saw him take advantage of an elite Red Sox defense to put up a 2.72 ERA. It did, however, come with a huge decrease in his strikeout rate, and that came after two seasons with a combined ERA of 4.07. He's almost always a must-start pitcher, but it often feels like you can't fully trust him. Of course, with an ADP around 150 in early drafts, it doesn't really matter if you can fully trust him. Just roll him out there, hope the ERA is closer to 3.50 than 4.00 and don't overthink it. He's a nice rotation filler as long as you don't expect him to be an ace. --Chris Towers
David Bednar accepts Yankees' qualifying offer

This one comes as a mild surprise and makes me wonder if Bednar just really wanted to stay with a team that wasn't willing to give him a multi-year commitment. He's a 32-year-old closer, and while he has mostly been a very good one over the past six seasons, there have been enough bumps in the road along the way to make the risk for Bednar pretty obvious. But from a Fantasy perspective, Bednar safely looks like a top-12 closer now that he's returning to the Yankees. His strikeout rate regressed in 2026, but his swinging-strike rate was actually higher than the previous season, and none of his underlying metrics otherwise really tell the story of a pitcher in decline. He's somewhere shy of the elite tier of closers for Fantasy, but he's good enough (and secure enough in his role for a good team) to be worth drafting as your primary source of saves. --Chris Towers
Ryan Jeffers accepts Twins' qualifying offer

It was a mild surprise to see the Twins extend Jeffers the qualifying offer, but it's not a surprise to see him accept it. Jeffers is a solid starting catcher -- good enough to be worth a fair share of playing time from the DH spot but he isn't the kind of player who was likely looking at a bunch of $50-plus million offers either. It's why taking the $23.2 million qualifying offer (and becoming the highest-paid catcher in baseball by annual value!) makes some sense here.

It also keeps the status quo in line for Jeffers. He'll play a decent amount and be reasonably productive when he's out there, but Jeffers' apparent breakout in the first half of 2026 proved unsustainable as he settled in more or less where we've come to expect him to be. He's a good hitter for a catcher, but given the strength of the position, he's more of a solid No. 2 catcher option than a true difference maker. That's nice to have around when it comes at the cost of a pick around 200th overall, as it should in most leagues. --Chris Towers
Dustin May signs with White Sox

There might be some sticker shock here – "$50 million for a career 4.12 ERA pitcher who has never thrown 150 innings in a season?" – but that's just the market rate for pitchers who reach free agency with their arms attached. May has been viewed as someone with a lot of upside over the years, but I think we're past that point after he showed little more than mid-rotation abilities in two seasons split between the Dodgers, Red Sox, and Brewers. He's a nice rotation filler for the White Sox, but unless something drastic happens to change his profile, he's a better source of GIFs than Fantasy production at this point in his career. --Chris Towers
Jake Bauers signs with Red Sox

After a surprise breakthrough season in which the underlying data was as sparkling as the top-line production, the biggest concern for Bauers was whether he'd sign with an organization that would help or hinder his follow-up campaign. By most outward indicators, he chose poorly. Sure, he'll be thrilled to get $58 million over the next four years, but his expected home run number at Fenway Park, with its deep right field fence, was only 18, tied for worst among all 30 venues.

He also joins a crowd of five players for four spots -- that is, unless (or until?) the Red Sox trade Jarren Duran. Even if Bauers himself isn't the one to sacrifice at-bats because of it (and look, he's no sure thing, for as good as he was in 2026), the potential impact on Willson Contreras, Roman Anthony, Wilyer Abreu and Duran makes his arrival a net negative for Fantasy. Bottom line is that this signing only amplifies the natural skepticism for a late-career breakout and explains why Bauers barely ranks inside my top 30 outfielders. --Scott White
Emilio Pagan signs with Tigers

The Tigers weren't willing to pay Kenley Jansen $12 million to be their closer, declining his option at the start of the offseason, and then turned around and signed Pagan for about the same amount. Probably safe to assume, then, he's their new closer after serving in the same capacity for the Reds the past two years. His 2026 performance was solid overall, but he was particularly dominant after returning from an early hamstring injury, delivering a 1.88 ERA, 0.84 WHIP and 10.7 K/9 over his final 30 appearances. The home run issues that prevented him from becoming a closer earlier in his career remain acute. Still, if he was able to navigate the past two years in Cincinnati with them, for as homer-friendly as that environment is, he should be able to do the same in Detroit. He'll be a budget-friendly RP2 on Draft Day. --Scott White
Evan Phillips signs with the Braves

The first multi-year signing of the offseason wasn't a headline name, and Phillips seems likely to open the season as the setup man behind Robert Suarez with his new squad. But Phillips is being paid over $10 million a year on a three-year deal, which is a decent-sized investment for a non-closer and reflects the upside he once showed in a high-leverage role. He came back from his June 2025 Tommy John surgery to pitch effectively for the Dodgers in 2026, posting a 3.46 ERA over 26 innings. While the underlying data isn't quite as promising, he still missed a ton of bats and had good control. The velocity also bounced all the way back and then some, past pre-injury levels.

Assuming the Braves don't bring back Raisel Iglesias, Suarez is locked in as the closer coming off a 1.06 ERA, but seeing as he missed three months of the 2026 season with elbow discomfort, there's a non-zero chance Phillips figures into the ninth-inning situation at some point in 2027. He's not necessarily a name you need to know for Draft Day in most leagues, but Phillips could be very relevant in 2027 if things go sideways for Suarez in the way they so often do for pitchers in their mid-30s. --Chris Towers

articles.headline: Russia must avoid ‘any actions’ expanding war in Ukraine — Trump, NATO chief say after Mar-a-Lago meeting
keyFacts: President Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte met at Mar-a-Lago to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine and the conflict in Iran.
Trump and Rutte stated that Russia must avoid any actions expanding the war in Ukraine and urged a rapid peaceful resolution.
US officials are engaging in trilateral discussions with Russia and Ukraine on territorial and security issues to end the war.
body: President Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte agreed that Russia must steer clear of “any actions” that would expand the war in Ukraine during a Mar-a-Lago meeting on Wednesday.
The meeting was “outstanding” and “very impactful,” Trump and Rutte said in a joint statement released by the White House.
The “primary subjects” discussed at the president’s Palm Beach, Fla., estate were Russia’s war against Ukraine and the conflict in Iran.
Advertisement
The “record setting achievements” the two leaders accomplished at the last two NATO summits were also topics of discussion.

“We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible,” Trump and Rutte said.
Advertisement
Russia is widely believed to be deploying a strategy of knocking out Ukrainian energy infrastructure in an attempt to make the coming winter as brutal as possible and beat Kyiv into submission.

US officials have been engaging in trilateral discussions with their Russian and Ukrainian counterparts – focused on territorial and security issues – as part of an effort to end the bloodiest war in Europe since World War II.
Trump and Rutte said they also talked about “the importance of continuing to expand defense spending and investment in our industrial base, both in the United States and across NATO.”

articles.headline: 10 Classic Books Worth Reading Over and Over
keyFacts: Polygon published an article highlighting 10 classic books that offer new insights, hidden clues, and deeper appreciation when read a second time.
The article explains that rereading works like Crime and Punishment, The Catcher in the Rye, and The Giver shifts focus from the plot's ending to the author's craft and psychological depth.
The featured selections span various eras and genres, including Franz Kafka's The Trial, Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, and F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby.
body: Most of us treat classic literature like a checklist to conquer in high school or college and then never touch those books again. You power through the plot, underline a few quotes for a term paper, and move on to whatever else is new. The catch is that great books rarely reveal their most fascinating tricks on the first pass. When you already know the ending, your brain stops racing for answers and begins to notice the machinery holding all those mysteries and themes together. Suddenly, an unreliable narrator's sleight of hand becomes obvious, or a throwaway line in chapter two hits like a freight train in light of later developments.

When you reread classic literature, everything changes: you stop rushing toward the finale and focus instead on how the author pulled it all off. Whether they reshape your perspective as you age or hide their best clues in plain sight, these 10 books reward you on every return trip.
10 Crime and Punishment (1866) by Fyodor Dostoevsky

Following an impoverished former student who believes extraordinary individuals can commit terrible acts in service of a greater purpose, Fyodor Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment is a descent into the mind of a murderer slowly unraveling under the weight of his own conscience. At the story’s center is Rodion Raskolnikov, a desperate and isolated young man living in the squalid slums of St. Petersburg who sets out to prove his own moral superiority. After murdering a pawnbroker, he is consumed by paranoia and the unbearable weight of his own guilt.

Dostoevsky borrows the mechanics of a detective novel as he weaves Raskolnikov’s psychological fallout into the overriding mystery, setting aside the familiar detective-versus-killer plot to peer into the killer’s mind. When you aren't racing through its pages to see whether Raskolnikov gets caught by the investigator Porfiry Petrovich, you savor the cat-and-mouse mind games between them. Every feverish rationalization and defensive outburst reads like a man slowly building his own prison cell.
9 The Trial (1825) by Franz Kafka

Franz Kafka's The Trial is one of those rare books that becomes more unsettling the older you get. Josef K. is a bank employee who is suddenly arrested by an inexplicable authority for a crime that is never identified, though he is not confined to a conventional prison. Instead, Josef has to navigate a secretive court system whose offices occupy cramped attics in a residential neighborhood while trying to defend himself against charges nobody will explain. He appears before an unruly crowd of onlookers at a hearing and consults a bedridden lawyer named Herr Huld, who never seems to make any progress on his case.

Kafka's masterpiece is a nightmare about institutional powerlessness, highlighting the absurdity of bureaucracy. It’s a compelling read, a piece of fiction that proves the systems governing our lives can be profoundly irrational. Its themes have only become more relevant with time, rewarding a second read once you stop looking for a logical explanation to the plot and start noticing Josef as he slowly pieces together the irrational system at play.
8 The Catcher in the Rye (1951) by J.D. Salinger

Few narrators divide readers quite like Holden Caulfield, a grieving teenager wandering through Manhattan in a red hunting hat after getting kicked out of yet another prep school. Across three wandering days in The Catcher in the Rye, J.D. Salinger lets Holden complain endlessly about the “phoniness” around him while quietly exposing the trauma and loneliness driving his cynicism.

Reading the novel in high school usually feels like an act of rebellion, as readers side with a misunderstood kid, but coming back to it as an adult transforms the entire experience. Holden's defensive anger turns into a heartbreaking portrait of a boy terrified of growing up in the wake of losing his younger brother. Even the adults in the story land differently on a second pass, shifting from out-of-touch villains to exhausted people trying to keep a spiraling teenager from falling off a cliff.
7 Heart of Darkness (1899) by Joseph Conrad

Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness turns a riverboat expedition into a suffocating descent into human cruelty. The novella follows Charles Marlow, a British sailor hired to pilot a steamer up the Congo River to retrieve Kurtz, a highly successful ivory trader who has cut off contact and turned a remote outpost into his personal kingdom.

As Marlow pushes deeper into the stark jungle, the supposed civility of his European employers slowly gives way, revealing unchecked greed and violence. On first pass, it’s easy to get swept up in the atmospheric writing and mystery surrounding Kurtz, which is why rereading it feels like stepping into a completely different story. Knowing how the journey ends makes every return trip that much more fascinating, turning Conrad's fog-choked prose into a trail of clues about Marlow's own complicity.
6 The Great Gatsby (1925) by F. Scott Fitzgerald

There are plenty of novels that explore the pursuit of the American Dream, but few understand its inherent contradictions quite like F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby. Set during the Roaring Twenties, the plot mostly centers on Jay Gatsby, the mysterious and wealthy neighbor of Nick Carraway, the story’s narrator. Gatsby’s lavish parties conceal an obsessive desire to reunite with his former love, Daisy Buchanan, but hiding beneath all the champagne, extravagant cars, and glittering excess is a deeply tragic story about the impossibility of recapturing the past.

Fitzgerald's writing is top-notch, while the characters remain endlessly fascinating. It’s no surprise The Great Gatsby has remained recommended reading for years, offering a sharp critique of the American Dream whose subtle clues hit much harder once you already know how Gatsby's story ends.
5 The Sun Also Rises (1926) by Ernest Hemingway

The Sun Also Rises is Ernest Hemingway's portrait of a generation struggling to find meaning in the aftermath of World War I. The protagonist, Jake Barnes, is an American journalist part of a circle of expatriate friends who drift through Paris and Spain in a haze of heavy drinking and late-night parties as they attempt to escape hidden emotional wounds.

At the center of the story is Jake's complicated relationship with Lady Brett Ashley, a woman he loves but cannot fully be with because of a war injury that has left him impotent. Hemingway's famously restrained prose gives the book much of its power on a second read, letting you catch the quiet heartbreak and disillusionment buried beneath seemingly ordinary conversations, a hallmark of Hemingway’s craft.
4 Pride and Prejudice (1813) by Jane Austen

Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice is one of the most enduring romantic novels ever written, and there's a reason readers keep returning to it more than two centuries after its publication. Set in rural Regency-era England, the story follows a sharp-witted young woman named Elizabeth Bennet navigating the expectations of English society while attempting to find a suitable marriage without sacrificing her independence. Her complicated relationship with the wealthy and aloof Mr. Darcy provides the foundation for an entertaining social satire that skewers class obsession and the assumptions we make about other people.

Much like The Sun Also Rises, the dialogue in Pride and Prejudice is razor-sharp, while Austen’s characters are wonderfully realized. Her observations about human behavior prove remarkably timeless, with every reread revealing how subtly she signals Darcy's early affection despite his stiff manners. It's a delightful book that never seems to lose its charm, and only gets better the more times you experience Elizabeth's stubbornness.
3 A Tale of Two Cities (1859) by Charles Dickens

A Tale of Two Cities is an enormous historical drama set against the backdrop of the French Revolution, following characters caught between the political upheaval of Paris and the relative stability of London. At its center is Charles Darnay, a French aristocrat attempting to escape his family's violent legacy, and Sydney Carton, a disillusioned English lawyer whose love for Darnay's wife, Lucie, places him on a path toward an extraordinary act of sacrifice.

Charles Dickens brings the chaos and brutality of revolutionary France to life while weaving together a deeply moving story about the possibility of personal transformation. It's a sweeping, emotionally powerful novel that builds toward one of literature's most unforgettable conclusions. Knowing the finale changes how every preceding chapter reads, making Sydney Carton's early apathy and reckless drinking feel like quiet clues to the man he would inevitably become.
2 Siddhartha (1922) by Hermann Hesse

Set in ancient India, Siddhartha tracks a young man who abandons his privileged upbringing to pursue spiritual enlightenment. Along the way, he tests himself through asceticism, material wealth, and romantic love, while seeking guidance from seasoned teachers, gradually discovering that no outside philosophy can provide him with the answers he seeks.

What makes Siddhartha so unforgettable on a reread is how it frames personal growth as something messy rather than linear. Real change often requires stumbling into failure or temptation first, forcing you to deal with immediate consequences before you can recognize what actually matters. It is a brisk read built for repeated visits, yet its lessons hold up across a lifetime.
1 The Giver (1993) by Lois Lowry

On the surface, Jonas lives in a peaceful utopia where hunger, suffering, and social conflict have largely been eradicated, yet that stability depends on stripping away emotional depth, collective memory, and individual choice. At the Ceremony of Twelve in Lois Lowry's The Giver, Jonas is chosen as the next Receiver of Memory rather than receiving a standard community assignment. His training with the old Receiver introduces him to sensations the rest of the community never experiences, from sled rides in deep snow to the warmth of sunshine and the shock of physical agony.

As Jonas absorbs such memories, he begins seeing cracks in his orderly world, especially as he notices flashes of color and questions the community's treatment of Gabriel, a young child who has been marked for release. Rereading The Giver makes the quiet dread much sharper because you already know what "release" actually means long before Jonas pieces it together. The polite rituals of the “evening telling of feelings” and the community’s calm routines seem less like signs of peace than evidence of a society sedated into forgetting what it gave up. Lowry trusts younger readers with heavy moral questions without ever talking down to them. Returning to the book years later hits differently because the horror shifts away from the shocking twists toward the quiet complicity of the adults who willingly traded away their humanity just to feel safe.

articles.headline: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
keyFacts: The US announced new import tariffs targeting China, the European Union, and 12 other jurisdictions following trade practice investigations.
China faces the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, while other countries face rates of up to 35%, 25%, or 20%.
The new duties are expected to take effect next year after undergoing public consultation, hearings, and potential legal challenges.
body: - Published
The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.

The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.
The White House began investigating the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with others facing either 20% or 25%.
The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the proposed tariffs together with extensive reports of how each jurisdiction's trade practices purportedly impact American commerce.
The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings.
Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of a good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing products.
Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.
The proposed tariffs will affect goods from China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.
The USTR's Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".
He said that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression".
They also employ "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America's manufacturing base", Greer said.
But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.
Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.
Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.
Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.
These new levies are build on a "stronger legal foundation" under US law compared with Trump's April 2025 Liberation Day tariffs, Singapore Management University economics lecturer Chang Pao-Li said.

Trump previously invoked emergency presidential powers to impose tariffs that have since been struck down, while his latest approach relies on the USTR's authority to impose tariffs to address certain foreign trade practices, she said.
The levies are still likely to face legal challenges, but there has been a "historical precedent" for such tariffs remaining in force, Chang said.

Many tariffs imposed under Section 301 - a law that allows the US to probe and retaliate against foreign trade practices - during Trump's first term remained in effect during his successor Joe Biden's administration.

However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer.

"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.
The additional tariff burden is likely to be small because a limited number of goods are subject to the new duties, Brown added.
Jurisdictions affected by the new wave of tariffs have voiced their disapproval over the Trump administration's move.
Washington has also proposed a 10% tariff on goods from Brazil, as part of a separate investigation over what it says are "harmful trade practices" undercutting American workers.
Brazilian authorities expressed their "outrage" at the announcement, saying that the move is aimed at pressuring the government to change regulations around issues like digital trade.
The South American nation faces duties on finished aircraft and sugar sold to the US.
"Brazil will not yield to such threats," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's office said.
The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.
The latest tariff rate is "not consistent" with the reality of bilateral economic-trade cooperation between the US and Vietnam, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Bui Thanh Son said.

The Japanese government said the US tariffs were "regrettable", while the Singapore government said it disagrees with the White House's findings and that it is engaging the USTR to explore ways to reduce the tariff.
South Korea's trade minister said the proposed 15% tariff will be "more than a decent outcome" as it would fall in line with a previously agreed limit with Washington.
Last year, Seoul pledged $350bn (Â£267bn) in US investments in exchange for lower tariffs as part of a trade deal.

US trading partners have been "waiting for this shoe to drop" and have argued that they are being wrongly accused of producing too much, said the Asia Society Policy Institute's Wendy Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator.
"Many believe that China, not them, should be the target for US action," she added.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun described the new tariffs as a form of "political manipulation", describing as "false" the US claim that China produces more than it can consume.
The tariff announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.
The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.
Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.
Beijing has remained vague on how it will respond but for now seems "prepared to live with the new rates provided they don't exceed 20%", Cutler said.
Additional reporting by Leehyun Choi in Seoul

articles.headline: EPA chief credits Stephen Miller with Iowa blast success: ‘He took the reins’
keyFacts: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin credited White House chief of staff Stephen Miller for leading the success of the Army's detonation of lead azide in Iowa.
FEMA issued an all-clear and lifted the area shelter-in-place after air monitoring showed no detectable lead following the blast.
Federal officials stated that they will remain on the ground in Iowa to share further air quality sampling results.
body: White House chief of staff Stephen Miller is to be credited for the success behind the Army’s detonation of 5 tons of destabilized lead azide in Iowa , according to Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin.

“I have to give credit where credit is absolutely due: the new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller. He took the reins on this over the course of the weekend. It was just conference call after conference call after conference call,” Zeldin said on Fox News’s Hannity on Wednesday evening.

Zeldin credited Miller just hours after the Federal Emergency Management Agency issued an “all-clear” and lifted the shelter-in-place for the area surrounding the blast at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Iowa state officials had expected the mandate to stay indoors to last for between 24 and 48 hours, but it only lasted for around 12 hours.
The EPA chief said over the weekend he was getting off a call with Miller about the planned blast that lasted until 11:30 p.m. on Sunday night.

“He was getting on another conference call afterwards, asking every possible question to make sure that we’ve considered all options, every option inside of government and out, every expert talking to make sure this was a success, and it was,” Zeldin said of Miller.

Several federal entities, including FEMA, the Army, and the EPA, released a joint statement Wednesday when the shelter-in-place was lifted, crediting both Miller and President Donald Trump for the effort.

“Under the steady leadership of President Trump and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, experts from our agencies jointly determined that a controlled, mitigated detonation during optimal weather conditions was the safest way to address the threat. We worked together seamlessly to plan, carry out, and monitor the situation,” they said in the statement.
The federal officials said Wednesday evening that the available air monitoring results showed no detectable lead, leading to FEMA’s “all clear.”

Zeldin also added that Trump was “asking all of the right questions” when he was briefed on the situation, with Zeldin calling the mitigation of the lead plume “the product” of that response from Trump and Miller.
In his own response to Wednesday’s events, Miller gave a shoutout to Zeldin.
ARMY DETONATES ENTIRE STOCKPILE OF DESTABILIZED LEAD AZIDE IN IOWA. EPA RELEASES PLUME TRACKERS

“I want to again express to the American public what a spectacular job the team assembled by President Trump executed in Iowa: Secretaries [Pete] Hegseth, [Robert F.] Kennedy [Jr.], [Brooke] Rollins and [Chris] Wright, Director [Robert] Cekada & Administrators [Cameron] Hamilton, [Jared] Isaacman and Zeldin (who has lifted the EPA to new heights),” Miller wrote on X.
The Trump administration agencies said federal officials will continue to remain on the ground in Iowa and will share further air quality sampling results as they come in.

articles.headline: India’s government ponders cradle to grave AI oversight
keyFacts: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi proposed an AI app to track children's data from age three to guide their education and career paths.
Uttar Pradesh has proposed building an AI Stack to link household data for social media monitoring, grievance detection, and various state services.
The Internet Freedom Foundation expressed concern that the proposed systems lack explicit legislative authorization and necessary oversight measures.
body: Indian politicians have proposed that AI could take a major role in citizens’ lives, partly through pervasive surveillance.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi last week spelled out his vision for an AI-based app that would collect data about children as they grow and analyze it to determine their aptitude for different types of study or careers.

Modi suggested that parents of three-year-old children should enter data about their offspring’s activities and accomplishments into a government-run system that is also accessible to teachers and even a child’s friends. Those records, the PM suggested, will “help identify children's interests and aptitude from an early age and redirect them in the study of their choice in future.”

That’s not an entirely creepy idea, because gaining access to India’s top tertiary institutions requires students to pay a hefty fee to sit for entrance exams. Modi pitched recommendations from the AI-powered app as something parents will appreciate as they contemplate whether to fund their offspring’s studies.
India’s most populous state, Uttar Pradesh (UP), has proposed to build an “AI Stack” to serve its 240 million-plus residents.

A 178-page tender seeks bidders to build a system that uses the state’s Family ID – a unique identifier for each household – to link data held by multiple agencies so it can be put to work in a dozen AI use cases.

One of those use cases is a tool for “AI-Enabled Social Media Monitoring and Urban Grievance Detection” that “analyses publicly available social media content including online news channels and connected grievance channels to detect emerging urban issues, citizen complaints, service interruptions, and recurring service gaps.”

The government wants that system to autonomously route complaints to relevant agencies, to automate actions like sending crews to patch up damaged roads. Critics have pointed to vague wording in the tender as potentially allowing the UP government to link this system to other agencies – a matter of concern given Indian state and national governments have implemented internet shutdowns to stop protestors from communicating on social media services and messaging apps.

Another use case is a knowledge assistant for state police that looks up case histories and other data but can’t use it to assess evidence or provide investigative conclusions. An app for teachers will advise them on how to create custom content to meet students’ needs. Healthcare workers would also get an app to help them make recommendations during patient visits.
Citizens get natural language interfaces to a system that offers advice on how to identify and access government services and schemes.
UP wants to drive these apps with self-hosted open-weight models, and to use only anonymized datasets.

India’s Internet Freedom Foundation worries that the systems described in the tender aren’t explicitly authorized by any legislation, and that the document doesn’t mention important oversight measures for the AI Stack. ®

body: Searching for a new display to take your gaming to the next level? XR glasses have a lot of potential, packing what looks like a massive display into a compact pair of glasses you can take with you almost anywhere. For Black Friday , Viture has some of its lowest prices ever with discounts on its Luma series of glasses and even its new flagship Viture Beast glasses, which earned a “Great” rating in our review.
Black Friday Deals on Viture XR Glasses

The Viture Beast landed this year at $549, but they’re on sale for $489 through Cyber Monday. Our reviewer, Jacqueline Thomas, said in her review, “the Viture Beast XR glasses are a great way to kick back on a flight and play games on a handheld without having to hold up a bulky device the entire way.”

These are the flagship glasses from the brand, offering some substantial tech inside. The Virture Beast pack in a pair of 1200p Micro-OLED displays that run at 120Hz. If that sounds like a brilliant recipe for gaming to you, you’ve clearly been doing your homework on display technology. The OLED displays give you rich contrast — especially with the 1,250-nit peak brightness — vivid color, and fast pixel response times on top of the fluid visual you already get from that refresh rate. The extra brightness of the displays can help if you’re using the glasses out in the daylight, but if you want to maximize the clarity, Viture uses electrochromic dimming that can cut down on external light.

The Viture Beast supports a lot of different use cases, working with phones, computers, and gaming handhelds alike. With adapters, they can work with consoles as well. You can set them up to run as a heads-up display always front and center or even virtually pin the display in space as if it were a monitor mounted in the real world.

They also all include electrochromatic dimming to let you see through them or darken your surroundings in a snap. If you wear glasses, this series is probably for you, since they include hardware focus adjustments to adapt for myopia.

The Luma is the simplest, offering a 50-degree field of view and sticking to the basics as a display. The Luma Pro stretches the field-of-view slightly, adds in some stylish lighting effects, and adds in a camera for extra spatial capabilities. The Luma Ultra goes yet another step further, upgrading to brighter panel and bringing even more cameras for additional spatial capabilities and hand tracking.

In addition to the savings on the Beast and Luma series, Viture is offering a free 8BitDo Ultimate 2C controller with the purchase of its glasses. It’s also discounting the Pro Mobile Dock to $99 , which gives the glasses extra battery, connectivity options, and can connect to HDMI sources. articles.headline: Fast Fashion Fiasco: Shein to Pay $100 Million in FTC Complaint
keyFacts: The Federal Trade Commission ordered Shein to pay 100 million dollars over allegations of deceptive practices involving shipping, customer service, and hidden negative reviews.
The FTC stated that Shein misled consumers about its products and suppliers while employing only five customer service agents for millions of US packages.
Under the proposed order, Shein must compensate customers, stop hiding negative reviews, improve customer service, and cease inaccurate delivery advertising.
body: Shein, one of the biggest fast-fashion brands in the world, has been ordered to pay $100 million by the Federal Trade Commission, which alleges that the Singapore-based online retail giant engaged in deceptive practices that left millions of US customers dissatisfied with its products and policies.

The FTC complaint alleges that Shein failed to follow through on its swift shipping policies, made it difficult for customers to resolve purchase issues and stifled negative customer reviews from seeing the light of day.

The complaint also alleges problems with the company’s supply chain, false information about the origin of the cotton used in its clothes, a failure to communicate shipping updates to customers and a lack of support for those whose packages were late or went missing altogether.
More from CNET

“The company misled millions of consumers about its products, its suppliers and the authenticity of its customer reviews,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Shein has ballooned over the past decade into the ultra-fast-fashion brand we know today, thanks in large part to the impact influencers have had on social media, posting videos trying on clothing supplied by the company.

In 2026, the company is estimated to ship roughly 1 million packages to US customers daily, according to the FTC. That number becomes even more astounding when you consider that Shein, the FTC alleges, employed just five customer service agents to answer calls from American customers.

This isn’t the first time Shein has faced negative scrutiny. Over the years, the company has faced allegations of numerous workers’ rights violations and is the largest polluter in the fast-fashion industry.

According to Yale Climate Connections, the company emitted 16.7 million total metric tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere in 2023. Comparatively speaking, that’s more than the pollution output of four coal power plants. Shein has since pledged to improve its treatment of workers and reduce carbon emissions, but scrutiny persists.

The $100 million will be used to compensate customers. And according to the FTC’s proposed order, the company, which earned roughly $50 billion in revenue in 2025, will not be able to continue advertising inaccurate shipping and delivery times; negative reviews will no longer be hidden; and its customer service offering will be bolstered.

“The agreement does not constitute an admission of liability, and we continue to disagree with aspects of the FTC’s characterization of our business and compliance practices,” a Shein spokesperson told CNET.

articles.headline: Mario, Pikachu, And Other Gaming Icon Balloons Won’t Be Flying This Thanksgiving
keyFacts: GameSpot reported that the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been delayed due to rain and windstorm forecasts.
The publication noted that past parade weather incidents resulted in balloon accidents and bystander injuries.
GameSpot stated that the delayed balloons are now scheduled to fly on Saturday at 8:30 AM ET.
body: New York City is no stranger to bad weather, be it blazing-hot summers, snow-packed winters, or fierce windstorms. Unfortunately for countless families who have made it a holiday tradition to turn on the TV and watch giant totems of pop culture sail in the streets of the great city, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been officially delayed due to a forecast of rain and windstorms--a first in its 100-year history.

In recent years, gaming icons have become more and more prominent during the parade. Beginning in 1993, a balloon of Sonic the Hedgehog marked the first game character to float among the procession. Since then, more characters have joined the festivities, including Mario, Pac-Man, Pikachu, and even Red the Angry Bird, among others.

However, those who have followed the history of Macy's balloons know that the mix of bad weather and massive, floating objects can result in genuine danger for balloon handlers, bystanders, and objects on the streets. Rather infamously, Sonic's 1993 appearance was marred by an incident where the balloon got stuck on a lamppost, popping the balloon and injuring two bystanders.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DmTC0m7wQbs

Other balloon bursts have proved even more catastrophic, with a series of mishaps in 1997 leading to a Cat in the Hat balloon causing injuries that left a woman comatose for days . Since then, more emphasis has rightfully been put on safety.

While it might be disappointing to not be able to point at the TV and go "Mario!" with your younger cousins around the TV tomorrow, the balloons will get a chance to fly on Saturday starting at 8:30 AM ET, when the weather is likely to be significantly less awful. You can find other ways to fill the time--but maybe ask your relatives first if it's okay to let the kiddos watch you play GTA 6.
