articles.headline: Denny’s Posts Statement Celebrating Jensen Huang’s Return As Nvidia CEO: ‘Some Things You Just Don’t Take Off The Menu’
keyFacts: Denny's posted a statement on Wednesday celebrating Jensen Huang returning as Nvidia CEO after his brief resignation earlier this month.
The diner chain highlighted Huang's past employment at Denny's and the booth where he and co-founders discussed the idea that became Nvidia.
Denny's statement omitted any mention of Huang's reported affairs, employee treatment, or the political lobbying involved in his reinstatement.
body: I’ve been playing a lot of Grand Theft Auto 6 lately, so I had to double-check that a recent post by the diner chain Denny’s was actually real and not some Rockstar-created satire. But no, Denny’s actually posted a 200+ word statement that is basically the company expressing how happy it is that Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia following his resignation earlier this month after it was reported that he’d cheated on his wife with an alleged spy and other women.
“Some things you just donât take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them,” is how Denny’s kicked off its statement posted on social media on Wednesday.

“Long before Nvidia changed the world, Jensen was washing dishes and serving guests at Dennyâs. Years later, he and his co-founders sat down over coffee in one of our booths to talk through the idea that became Nvidia. We couldnât be prouder of the history we share,” posted the diner chain.

In the rest of the statement, Denny’s referenced a plaque that had been removed from the booth where Huang and those founders sat many years ago. It explained that once Denny’s leadership learned about its removal, it quickly had the plaque put back up “where it belongs.” The company further explained that Huang’s history with Denny’s goes beyond that meeting and back to the “dishes he washed, the guests he served and the work he still talks about with pride.”
Every story starts somewhere. Weâre proud to be part of Jensenâs. pic.twitter.com/WpWJdLFmIs
— Dennyâs (@DennysDiner) November 25, 2026
It’s a very deranged and hard-to-comprehend social media post from a chain of diners that serve subpar breakfast food. Denny’s ain’t Waffle House, that’s for sure.

The rest of the incredibly silly statement goes on to mention all the people who have worked at Denny’s in the past and how they all matter to the company. “One of them,” it says, “went on to change the world, and he still remembers what he learned at the sink.”

Nowhere in the statement does Denny’s acknowledge Huang’s multiple reported affairs, one of which involved an alleged Chinese spy. It also doesn’t mention the reportedly terrible ways he treated his employees at Nvidia, nor does it take note of how his recent return as CEO on November 23 was only made possible after members of the United States government, including President Trump, allegedly lobbied hard for his reinstatement.Â Many of them, including Trump, have a large chunk of their cash invested in Nvidia, a company that controls the future of AI thanks to its death grip on the chips needed to build data centers.
“Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffeeâs on. Weâre always open, 24/7,” ended Denny’s statement.

articles.headline: 2nd Circuit deals blow to Manhattan DA, breathes new life into Trump's hush money appeal
keyFacts: A federal appeals court revived Donald Trump's bid to move his New York hush money case from state court to federal court.
The 2nd Circuit panel ruled that a lower judge made legal errors when denying Trump's second transfer request following his conviction.
The appeals panel requested that New York courts suspend further proceedings while the federal jurisdiction dispute is resolved by Judge Lewis J. Liman.
body: A federal appeals court handed President Donald Trump a legal victory Monday, reviving his bid to wrest his New York hush money case from state court and potentially overturn his felony conviction on presidential immunity grounds.

The 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that an August decision by the late U. S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein, a Clinton appointee who died in October, that denied Trump's second transfer bid was improper.

The criminal case centered on Trump's reimbursement of his then-attorney Michael Cohen, who paid adult film actress Stormy Daniels $130,000 shortly before the 2016 election to keep her from publicizing an alleged sexual encounter with Trump a decade earlier.
Trump, who denies the encounter, was found guilty in May 2024 of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records.
FEDERAL APPEALS COURT REFUSES TO REHEAR TRUMP APPEAL OF $83M E JEAN CARROLL DEFAMATION JUDGMENT

At his January 2025 sentencing — days before his second inauguration — Trump received an unconditional discharge, leaving him with no prison time or fine, though the felony conviction remains on his record.
Trump has continued fighting to move the case out of state court, scoring a victory before a three-judge appellate panel Monday.
"We disagree with the district court," said circuit judges Raymond J. Lohier Jr., an Obama appointee; José A. Cabranes, a Clinton appointee; and John M. Walker Jr., a George H. W. Bush appointee.

The panel found Hellerstein made two legal errors: A federal official can still seek removal after being convicted, and Trump showed "good cause" to file a second removal notice. A full written opinion will follow "in due course," the judges wrote.

Trump's attorneys argued in a September brief that the legal landscape had fundamentally changed since his first attempt to transfer the case in 2023. They pointed to the Supreme Court's July 2024 immunity decision, arguing that Manhattan prosecutors had relied on evidence of Trump's presidential activities at trial that the high court subsequently deemed off-limits.

Trump attorney Robert Giuffra Jr. warned that leaving the case in New York's judicial system could significantly delay the president's ability to seek relief from the nation's highest court, arguing Trump "will likely have to wait years."
TRUMP'S LAWYERS PUT DEM AG ON NOTICE FOR TARGETING HIS FAMILY IN NY FRAUD FIGHT: 'CANNOT STAND'

Manhattan prosecutors had urged the 2nd Circuit to uphold Hellerstein's denial, arguing Trump engaged in "strategic delay" by testing his immunity claim in state court first and seeking a transfer only when he believed he would lose. They also maintained that falsifying business records over a personal payoff had nothing to do with official duties.

The ruling puts the question of federal jurisdiction before U.S. District Judge Lewis J. Liman, who inherited the case after Hellerstein's death. The appellate panel also requested that New York courts suspend further proceedings while the jurisdiction dispute is resolved.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

If Liman grants the transfer, the federal court will adopt the conviction, setting up a clash over whether it must be vacated under the Supreme Court's immunity standard. Moving the case would not allow Trump to pardon himself, however, because the underlying charges remain New York state offenses outside the reach of a presidential pardon .
Fox News Digital reached out to the Manhattan District Attorney's Office and Trump's legal team for comment but did not receive a response by publication time.

articles.headline: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
keyFacts: S&P Global Ratings is considering downgrading Nvidia from AA to AA- due to management, governance, and key man risks.
The review was triggered by concerns over weak executive oversight and heavy reliance on CEO Jensen Huang after his ouster and reinstatement, according to S&P.
S&P expects to finish its review within 90 days, which could raise Nvidia's borrowing costs and affect its financial guarantees for AI infrastructure projects.
body: S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.

Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement.
The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.

Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.

In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.
A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

articles.headline: European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment
keyFacts: NASA slammed a spacecraft into the asteroid Dimorphos in September 2022, successfully altering its trajectory and shortening its orbit.
Planetary scientist Sabina Raducan stated that the impact was successful and created a large mess that required further investigation.
The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft arrived and released images showing that the impact carved a stadium-sized crater on Dimorphos.
body: Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory.

Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid’s 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation.

But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next.

“We knew right away that the impact was successful, that DART made a really, really large mess,” said Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist at the International Space Science Institute in Bern, Switzerland. “However, we didn’t really know what kind of mess. We were still missing pieces of the puzzle.”
Following up

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft recently arrived in the vicinity of Didymos and Dimorphos after a two-year journey from a launch pad in Florida. On Wednesday, ESA released Hera’s first views of the scar left by DART on Dimorphos. The images show the car-sized impactor carved out a crater the size of a stadium, nearly as big as Dimorphos itself, a rugged chunk of extraterrestrial rock measuring about 500 feet (151 meters) across.

Mission planners selected Didymos and Dimorphos for the deflection experiment because they are similar to many near-Earth asteroids, but there’s no risk of them striking our home planet. Scientists weren’t sure what Hera would find when it got to the double asteroid, currently orbiting the Sun about 120 million miles (193.5 million kilometers) from Earth.

articles.headline: Trump just can’t quit tariffs
keyFacts: The Trump administration announced potential new tariffs targeting dozens of countries, including China, South Korea, and European Union member states.
The administration justified tariffs using an investigation into alleged unfair trade practices after courts struck down previous global tariff attempts.
US trade adviser Jamieson Greer said the new tariffs are unlikely to take effect sooner than a couple of months from now.
body: President Donald Trump at the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardoning ceremony at the White House on November 24, 2026. | Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images
This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here .
Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is trying to keep its trade war alive with new tariff announcements.

Who’s getting tariffed? Potentially dozens of countries, including China, the EU’s 27 member states, South Korea, and others. If they take effect, the China tariffs would start at 20 percent and could escalate to as high as 40 percent, while EU tariffs would start at 15 percent and could go up from there.

How? The administration is justifying these tariffs on the basis of an investigation into what it alleges are unfair trade practices by the targeted countries — a step it’s taking only after its previous tariffs regime, which attempted to use emergency powers to impose tariffs, was struck down by the Supreme Court.

Despite Wednesday’s announcement, it’s still not entirely clear when the new tariffs will take effect; according to the US trade adviser , Jamieson Greer, it’s unlikely to be sooner than “a couple months from now.”

What’s the context? Courts have struck down two different attempts by the Trump administration to impose a global tariff regime, including the emergency authority the Supreme Court ruled on in February 2026.

Wednesday’s move is part of its attempt to reconstitute that regime using other authorities, joining a sweeping set of tariffs imposed in July over alleged forced-labor concerns. The US is also engaged in a specific trade fight with Canada: In August, President Donald Trump imposed 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian goods after trade talks fell through.

Why does this matter? Tariffs, as my colleague Eric Levitz has reported , don’t work the way the president seems to think; his project is based on a fundamentally incorrect understanding of economics that’s making things more expensive for American consumers.

Despite that fact, Wednesday’s announcement suggests he’s doubling down, despite persistently high inflation , and undeterred by his crushing midterms defeat earlier this month, when voters motivated by affordability turned out to deliver a historic rebuke.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Hi readers, happy early Thanksgiving! This will be our last newsletter for the week — the Vox team is taking some time off to be with our families today and tomorrow, and we’ll see you back here on Monday.

Before we go, I have one more story to share from my colleague Jonquilyn Hill, who wrote about the best way to strategically approach your Thanksgiving dinner for maximum enjoyment (subjective, yes, but she asked a gastroenterologist for some tips). Plus: Why it’s not really the turkey that’s making you so sleepy. You can read it all here with a gift link — happy feasting!

articles.headline: The Fable reboot had to look beyond Lionhead's RPG trilogy because games like The Witcher 3 "became the gold standard"
keyFacts: Developer Playground Games looked beyond the original Fable trilogy for its reboot because games like The Witcher 3 raised player expectations.
Studio founder Ralph Fulton stated that games such as The Witcher 3 and modern Assassin's Creed titles redefined open-world action RPGs.
The Fable reboot will still draw heavily from Lionhead's original games, retaining British wit, a morality system, and life simulation elements.
body: Developer Playground Games had to look beyond Lionhead's original run of Fable games when rebooting the classic fantasy series, and it's all thanks to games like The Witcher 3, which changed what many players expect from their big RPGs and set a new "gold standard."

The upcoming Fable reboot is finally ending its decade-long development journey soon. Playground Games had to set up an entirely new team to work on its fairytale revival, so Fable's production wasn't quite as smooth sailing as the studio's consistently excellent Forza Horizon series, for example.

Asked about what's changed during that time, in an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, studio founder and general manager Ralph Fulton named technological advancements as a biggie, but the impact of other games was perhaps even greater.

"In 2015, The Witcher 3 redefined what an open-world action RPG looks like and became the gold standard," Fulton said. "And after that bar was raised, the Assassin's Creed franchise changed into this more modern iteration with Origins, Odyssey, and Valhalla, and became like a quasi-RPG."

"All of these games continue to reset player expectations," he continued. Millions of players suddenly had certain expectations about what their big-budget, open-world role-playing games should look like. So, Playground couldn't pull inspiration from Fable and Fable alone.
"I think looking only to the original Fable trilogy for inspiration would leave us lacking in terms of what the modern audience, the modern marketplace, expects," Fulton added.

Still, Playground's Fable is drawing most heavily from Lionhead's Fable. Fulton specifically mentions the game's signature British wit and in-flux morality system as examples. Then there's also the spontaneous life sim elements that "none of our competitors do," according to Fulton. "It's a totally Fable thing, the social simulation and economic simulation. Okay, there are games that have economic simulations, but they're not in [our] RPG category. Fable is unique in that it's almost like a life sim in terms of genre."

Raising four separate families and becoming the entire map's benevolent landlord was one of the funnest parts of Fable back in the day, alongside those sometimes silly characters. Seeing next year's Fable lean into those systemic choices, and having Albion's NPCs react to them more believably, could give this one a very long shelf life.

articles.headline: You can turn Claude artifacts into Windows and Mac apps now – here’s how
keyFacts: Anthropic is releasing a beta feature allowing users to install Claude artifacts as standalone desktop apps on Mac and Windows.
Anthropic said the desktop apps open in their own windows, require internet access, and need permission to interact with computers.
Users can install artifacts by opening Claude's Share menu, selecting the install option, and setting permissions as needed.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- You can install Claude artifacts as desktop apps, but they’ll need Wi-Fi.
- Be careful when giving artifact apps full computer access.
- Claude, a work tool in its own right, is spawning even more work tools.

Anthropic is making its Claude artifacts available as desktop apps, meaning you can share and more easily access your most-repeated tasks on your computer. The “install as app” feature is available in beta for all free and paid Claude plans and works on both Mac and Windows, but not Linux.

Anthropic first released artifacts in 2024. Since then, they’ve become a way to standardize and repeat tasks users do regularly, especially at work. Previously, artifacts ran via your Claude window or in a browser. By splicing them out as distinct desktop apps, you can now run different Claude queries while also using your artifacts locally, or use those apps without opening Claude at all.
More from ZDNET

“When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer,” Anthropic said.

Artifact apps can still access Claude and any connectors you’re using, and they update automatically when you edit the artifact itself in Claude. When apps request something from Claude, though, that goes toward your Claude usage limits, which are lowest for free users.
Anthropic said the app feature is meant to streamline building apps for both developer and non-developer work.

The update clarifies where AI software for work is headed. Claude is already more of an AI-powered work suite than a single helpful chatbot for many organizations. Evidently, people are using tools like artifacts frequently enough — and simultaneously with other Claude features — that they need those Claude-based tools to function like discrete bits of software on their own.
“If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention,” Anthropic said.
What are the limitations of Claude artifact apps?

Claude artifact apps don’t have the same functionality as apps you could build using Claude Code, though. Even if you don’t need Claude open for these apps to work, you’ll still need to be signed in to Claude and have internet access, so they’re not an entirely portable or off-grid option.

The feature’s support page also notes that legacy artifacts, “live artifacts from Claude Cowork,” and artifacts generated from templates like Docs, Slides, and Sheets can’t be installed as desktop apps.
How to install Claude artifacts as desktop apps on Mac and Windows

First, make sure Claude for Mac or Windows is updated. You can try the “install as app” feature, which is in beta for all free and paid plans, via Claude’s Share menu. Select the Install as app option, which will then download the artifact you chose to your desktop. From there, set permissions as needed.
- Open the artifact you want to install in Claude.
- Open Claude’s Share menu.
- Select the Install as app option, which will then download the artifact you chose to your desktop.
- Set permissions as needed.
How to manage Claude artifact app permissions
Permissions range from the default (whatever they are in a browser) to app-specific permissions like sending notifications and full computer access.

Full computer access means the artifact app can “run programs and read, change, or delete your files without asking each time,” Anthropic said, so proceed carefully. Every time you edit and update the artifact (and thus the app), Claude will ask you to confirm permissions again, so you’ll ideally have regular checkpoints to revise access. Still, there are some guardrails in place: Anthropic only lets you give full computer access to apps you’ve made yourself. For Team and Enterprise plans, that extends to any apps made by your coworkers.
“Anthropic doesn’t review apps before you install them, so only give full access to apps you trust,” the company said.
For Claude Enterprise plans, the install-as-app feature is off entirely until an admin turns it on in Organization settings.

articles.headline: Lawrence O'Donnell Has A Winning Explanation For Trump And His 'WTH' Midterms Talk
keyFacts: Donald Trump questioned recent midterm election results during a White House event, asking for an explanation of what occurred.
Lawrence O'Donnell cited Democrat Victoria Broderick's defeat of eight-term Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee to explain the election results.
O'Donnell said Trump will continue to be mystified by election results because Trump will not understand victories powered by everyday people.
body: Lawrence O’Donnell on Tuesday used one of Democrats’ major midterm upsets to respond to President Donald Trump’s joke about the red wipeout.

Trump — in remarks at the White House turkey pardoning ceremony earlier in the day — showed love to West Virginia turkey farmers Scott and Becky Rightsell before pivoting to talk about him winning the state by a margin of “45 points.” (Trump’s margin was slightly less in 2016, roughly 42 percentage points, and about 39 points in 2020.)
“I don’t know what happened. I won it by a lot. I don’t know what the hell happened with this last election. Somebody please explain it to me,” Trump said.
O’Donnell reacted, “This is peak Trumpian humility.”

The host stressed that Democrats had “more winners than we could keep track of” in this year’s election, pointing to Rep.-elect Victoria Broderick (D-Tenn.) defeating eight-term Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-Tenn.), becoming the first out pansexual person to be elected to Congress in the process.

He tossed to a Getty Images photo of Broderick — a tech support worker whose campaign spent a total of $90,000 on the campaign trail and didn’t run TV ads — smiling with her arms raised in the nation’s capital.
Election forecasters saw the seat as reliably red, and the results are a notable flip from 2024, when DesJarlais defeated Broderick by 43 points, O’Donnell noted, citing a New York Times article.
“She was outspent by a strongly financed Republican incumbent, and she shocked every political professional in Washington by winning. And she shocked herself,” the host said.
Broderick, in a post to social media, emphasized that she didn’t have the “political machine behind us.”
“We didn’t have corporate PAC money, we didn’t have powerful insiders. We had you, the people,” she wrote.
“That is an explanation that Donald Trump is not going to understand,” O’Donnell said.
“And so he will continue to be mystified about what the hell happened with this last election.”

articles.headline: A rising political star in China is the latest victim of Xi’s purge
keyFacts: Shanghai party chief Chen Jining is under investigation for suspected discipline and law violations, state media reported.
Chen is the fourth Politburo member purged in under two years amid President Xi Jinping's power consolidation effort.
The downfall comes ahead of next year's Communist Party Congress, where Xi is expected to extend his rule.
body: He was on the rise among China’s political elite, hosting tech leaders and senior American officials. But now Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s influential politburo, appears to be the latest senior official brought down by President Xi Jinping’s sweeping purge.

The hammer unexpectedly came down on Chen in the form of a two-line bulletin on the Xinhua news agency Tuesday: He is “suspected of serious violations of Party discipline and law and is currently under disciplinary review and supervisory investigation” — a common euphemism for corruption crackdowns on ruling Communist Party officials under Xi.
Public announcements such as these usually mark the end of a political career in China. Chen has made no public statement.

He is the fourth politburo member to be purged in less than two years, part of a broader crackdown that has swept aside top military leaders as Xi consolidates power. He is set to extend his rule next year, at a party congress that is held once every five years and looms over the preceding months.
But Chen’s abrupt downfall took many close observers of China by surprise, given his profile and career path would usually point to a bright future.

“He was potentially going to the highest level, which would be the standing committee. And I think from a lot of Western observers, people thought he had even better prospects,” Damien Ma, the Singapore-based director of the Carnegie China think tank, told NBC News.
Xi’s pursuit of loyalty

Some analysts have speculated that Xi, increasingly viewed as likely to rule for life, may have been purging a viable replacement. Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London, said however that Chen was “someone who could rise further but not as a successor.”

Chen, a 62-year-old technocrat known as a friend of foreign business and an advocate for AI, was an environmental scientist who studied in London and swiftly rose through the party’s ranks. He served as China’s environmental minister, Beijing’s mayor and the party secretary in Shanghai — a post once held by Xi and widely considered a stepping stone to bigger things.

Just last month, Chen hosted Apple Chairman Tim Cook, welcoming the U.S. tech giant to “make full use of Shanghai’s strengths” and bring more products to the city, a financial and cultural hub that has long served as a connection between China and the international community.
In his last public appearance last week, during a tour of a shipping facility, Chen called for advancing the industry’s digital transformation.
By Wednesday, Chen’s name has been removed from some official websites. A webpage on the Shanghai government site showing that meeting with Cook is now showing a 404 message, or not found.

Chen is just the latest senior official in the crosshairs of Xi’s long-running anti-corruption campaign and emphasis on party discipline, which analysts say is as much about loyalty as it is about reform.

“It is a warning to all technocrats, as Chen was a rising star among technocrats and had no apparent failures in a technocratic way. So, message is: adhere to strict party discipline and demonstrate unquestionable loyalty to Xi or else,” Tsang said.

The party’s Central Committee, which has about 200 mostly male leaders, vowed to “ensure more rigorous discipline enforcement, and make full use of discipline as a guide, restraint, guarantee, and incentive” at its closed-door gathering, the fifth plenum, last month.

“What they’ve been building as part of this discipline machine over the last 15 years is to kind of implement their sort of internal operating system of how they deal with, let’s say, bad eggs within the party,” Ma, of Carnegie China, said.

“The top leadership is normalizing this anti-corruption, this self-cleansing,” Ma said. “It is now a normal part of what the party expects, and they’re trying to embed that over time and down to every single level,” he added.

The Chinese government has not announced any charges against Chen, who was the youngest member of the country’s elite decision-making body. The 24-member Politburo was unveiled in 2022 but is now down to 21 members after the purges. Last month, top general Zhang Shengmin was elevated to the body in a rare addition.

Chen’s undoing comes a year before the party’s top leadership is reshuffled at the 21st Communist Party Congress, when Xi is expected to solidify control even further and cement another five-year term at the helm of the country.
From London to Shanghai

Born in 1964, Chen studied at the prestigious Tsinghua university, long a major pipeline for senior party officials and where he served as president from 2012 to 2015. His name has now been removed from Tsinghua’s online list of former presidents.
After studying at Tsinghua in the 1980s, he moved for a decade to Britain, where he obtained a doctorate from Imperial College London in 1993.
Chen returned to Tsinghua’s environmental science and engineering department in 1998 before being named the university’s president in 2012, according to an official biography.
He’s authored dozens of papers, including on carbon emission reduction and water quality monitoring.

The relatively young Chen would ride around campus on his bike and built a reputation for pushing institutional reforms in his three years at the helm of the university, according to an article in People’s Digest, a magazine affiliated with the People’s Daily, the community party’s official newspaper.

The article, titled “From University President to Cabinet Minister,” was published in 2015, the same year he was picked to lead the Environmental Protection Ministry. In 2017, Chen became mayor of the capital, Beijing, where he oversaw the 2022 Winter Olympics during the Covid pandemic.
Later that year he was transferred to Shanghai and became the party chief, a coveted role that Xi took on himself in 2007 before becoming the country’s leader in 2013.
There, he became heavily involved with the tech industry, regularly hosting CEOs and advocating for more investment into Shanghai, where the World AI Conference was hosted earlier this year.

Chen hosted Elon Musk in 2023 to discuss Tesla’s operations in the city. Last year, he accompanied Xi to an AI hub there. And last month, Chen met with several European tech leaders, in addition to hosting Cook.
Alongside the top post in Shanghai, Chen also was elected for a five-year term as a member of the Politburo, China’s elite decision-making body headed by Xi.
While the Politburo is not the absolute apex of power, he was seen as a contender the much-smaller Politburo’s Standing Committee, which is made up of the country’s highest ranking officials.

“If you’re party secretary of one of the four big municipalities, Beijing, Shanghai, Chongqing and Tianjin, you have pretty good prospects. That’s sort of an indication that you’re on your way up,” Ma said.

Whether or not Chen’s ousting deals a blow to the country’s technology ambitions and its race for dominance in artificial intelligence, remains to be seen, Ma said. But either way, his downfall will force a rethink among those seeking to predict the route to power in modern China.
“Part of it is thinking through what is really the new criteria to get to the top, and they may not be what we thought just a few months ago,” Ma added.

articles.headline: How American Thanksgiving took root -- and evolved -- in Liberia
keyFacts: American settlers brought Thanksgiving to Liberia in the 19th century, where the legislature later established it as a national holiday in 1883.
Liberians of various faiths celebrate the holiday by attending religious services in the morning and gathering for family meals featuring chicken, rice, and local stews.
Residents celebrate the holiday to express gratitude for freedom, divine protection, unity, and the harvest following periods of conflict in the country.
body: How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia
Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.
"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."
Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.

"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."

The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.

Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.
That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.
The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.
A sacred day for all
Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."

Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well

"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff, a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving. "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."
When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.
"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.
Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.
"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."
The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.
"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."

Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."
(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")
"I'm thanking God"

This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.

Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."
Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation, an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.
"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.
